Pulsed beeps (two per presentation, 25 ms soft edges) play in one ear at a time, 500 Hz to 8 kHz. PureEQ keeps one statistical model of your thresholds in every band and both ears, linked across frequency and between the ears. Each beep is played at the level expected to teach it the most, and a band is finished as soon as its threshold is known well enough. Silent beeps measure guessing, and the model allows for the odd slip. Missed a beep? Play it again once; the answer then counts as heard on either listen. About 2 minutes instead of 6.
From the listening check to EQ

Your thresholds are compared with a reference listener\'s through well-tuned headphones of your type (ISO 389-7 thresholds, Harman target). The difference covers your ears and your headphones together, which is what an EQ can fix. PureEQ corrects the smooth trend, not every point, measured from your low mids (500 Hz to 1.5 kHz), and only what the answers clearly show: small differences at 75 % (usually the headphones\' own sound), larger ones at about a third, so the sound stays natural. Bass below 400 Hz is left to your taste and treble boosts stop at +6 dB. Both ears share one filter set, and a difference between your ears counts only when the answers clearly show it, so voices stay centred.

Optionally, pick your model from AutoEq\'s database (over 6,000 headphones measured by oratory1990, crinacle, Rtings and others; AutoEq by Jaakko Pasanen, MIT licence). PureEQ downloads the model\'s measurement and corrects it the way AutoEq does: compared with the Harman target as measured on the same rig, smoothed and inverted, with gentle slopes, boosts limited to +6 dB, narrow notches left alone, and the target\'s own bass added back. Above about 5 kHz, where people\'s ears differ by 5 to 30 dB, only half of it applies. crinacle publishes only finished corrections, so those use AutoEq\'s own. The listening check\'s reference allows for the correction, so the measured response isn\'t corrected twice: the listening check then only fixes your ears and how the headphones sit. PureEQ remembers the model you picked for each pair of headphones.

The whole EQ\'s bass, from the correction, the listening check and your taste together, is kept within what it\'s worth. Over-ear headphones hold bass below 50 Hz near the 50 Hz level: little music lives down there, and a boost costs as much volume. Full sub-bass in Fine-tuning lifts this and says what it costs on your headphones. Sealed earbuds keep their deep bass. No headphones get more than +12 dB (over-ear) or +15 dB (in-ear) of bass over the mids.

Bass (a 105 Hz shelf, as in Harman\'s headphone research) and treble (a broad shelf from 2.5 kHz, the shape Harman\'s listeners adjusted) are tuned by blind A/B comparisons, each pair loudness-matched with the ITU BS.1770 weighting so louder never wins by default. PureEQ starts from Harman\'s three groups of listeners (most like the target, some want more bass, some less with a little more treble), learns from every answer, \"Same\" included, and picks each next pair to learn the most: usually 5 to 7 rounds. Each new pair is marked and waits until you\'ve heard both. Air (above 10 kHz), warmth and vocals are yours to set by hand.

PureEQ keeps on or off for each output: the phone speaker, each pair of headphones, a car or speaker. A profile is tuned for headphones, so the phone speaker starts off and plays untouched; switch it on there and that\'s kept too. Back on headphones it comes back on, with the profile you last used with them. \"All audio\" uses Android\'s DynamicsProcessing effect on the output mix with a separate curve for each ear, in fine bands (each FFT bin below 530 Hz, 1/16 octave above). The level is lowered only as much as music needs: treble boosts barely raise a mix\'s peaks, so they cost almost no loudness; a bass boost costs about its own size. Exports use AutoEq\'s formats, so Wavelet, Poweramp Equalizer, JamesDSP and Equalizer APO read them directly.

Your profiles and results stay on this phone, and in your Google account\'s encrypted backup if Android backup is on. The optional room check listens for 3 seconds to measure noise level and stores nothing. PureEQ only goes online to check for its own updates (a small update notice, then the new version when there is one) and, if you look up your headphones, to download AutoEq\'s public list and that model\'s correction from the jsDelivr or GitHub servers. Nothing about you or your results is sent.

Headphone data via AutoEq (Jaakko Pasanen, MIT licence), measured by oratory1990, Rtings, crinacle and others. PureEQ computes the correction from the measurement with AutoEq\'s method; crinacle publishes only finished corrections, so those are AutoEq\'s own, to AutoEq\'s target. The same model can be listed by several measurers; the first is usually the most trusted. Pick a variant (ANC on, passive…) if it matches how you listen.
